text: On 2026-05-11, the billing importer retried failed Stripe events for 47 minutes after the queue worker lost its lease. The draft postmortem says the incident was a seamless learning opportunity that strengthened our commitment to reliability. The evidence is narrower. The worker logs show repeated lease-renewal failures from 09:14 to 10:01 UTC. The team disabled retries at 10:07 UTC, replayed the affected events from a frozen export, and added a guard that blocks retry fan-out when lease renewal fails. The guard shipped behind feature flag BillingLeaseGuard on 2026-05-12. The remaining risk is that old exports before 2026-04-01 do not include merchant timezone, so the replay tool still needs manual review for that subset. The customer note must not promise that the problem cannot recur. It can say that the specific retry fan-out path is now blocked and that the affected invoices were reviewed. The longer draft also repeats that the team learned a great deal, that collaboration improved, and that the event created momentum for future quality work. Those claims are not supported by the evidence in the incident log. The useful material is the chain of events, the customer-visible effect, the mitigation, and the remaining replay risk. It should also avoid turning the incident into a brand story. The audience needs to know what happened, what changed, and what still needs manual review. The output should keep the exact operational boundary and resist a cleaner but less accurate ending. If a sentence can be removed without losing a fact, condition, consequence, or remaining risk, the sentence is padding. It should leave room for the remaining limitation and avoid any sentence whose only job is reassurance. The operational facts are enough.
